summary: This standards-track document defines the cid: and mid: URL schemes, which refer to parts of a mail message or to messages by identifier. For example, an HTML part can point to another part of the same message. It was replaced by RFC 2392.

plainLanguage.summary: RFC 2111 defines cid: and mid: URLs for referring to email messages and their body parts. A cid: URL points to a part by its Content-ID, while a mid: URL can point to a whole message or a part within it.

subtitle: URL schemes for referring to email messages and their MIME body parts.

tldr.problem: A message may need to refer to a body part inside itself or to another message, such as when HTML refers to an included image.
tldr.mechanism: A cid: URL identifies a body part by Content-ID; a mid: URL identifies a message and can optionally add a Content-ID to identify a part within it.
tldr.outcome: RFC 2111 defined the schemes and was obsoleted by RFC 2392.

facts.label: mid: URL with a part identifier

sections.title: Why Email Needs These URL Schemes
sections.content:
A MIME email can contain a web page and related resources such as images. The page needs a way to refer to those body parts. A Content-ID URL, written cid:, provides that reference.

A Message-ID URL, written mid:, refers to an email or news message. It can also identify a body part within a named message.
sections.plainLanguage: An HTML part in an email can refer to another part in the same message. A mid: URL can also identify a message or a part inside another message.

sections.title: The cid: and mid: Forms
sections.content:
A cid: URL contains a Content-ID and refers to a specific body part, generally another part in the same message as the reference. A mid: URL contains a Message-ID; by itself it refers to the message, and with a slash followed by a Content-ID it refers to a body part within that message.

Characters that are not allowed in a URL must be encoded with the percent-hex escape form. The RFC requires support for the long mid: form containing both the message ID and content ID.
sections.plainLanguage: Use cid: plus a part's identifier to refer to a body part. Use mid: plus a message identifier for a message, or add a part identifier for a specific part inside it.

sections.title: Referencing an Image or Earlier Message
sections.content:
The RFC's first example is a multipart message with an HTML body part and an image body part. An IMG reference in the HTML uses a cid: URL matching the image part's Content-ID.

A second example uses a mid: URL containing both a message identifier and a content identifier to refer to a particular part in a previous message.
sections.plainLanguage: An email's HTML can use a cid: URL to name an image included in the same message. A mid: URL can identify a part in an earlier message.

sections.title: Security and Identifier Disclosure
sections.content:
The RFC says these URLs provide addressing or referencing and disclose no more about the originator's environment than the corresponding Message-ID and Content-ID values.

If that information could be confidential, the message originator must take precautions to prevent its disclosure. The RFC notes that the same precautions should already apply to ordinary use of those identifiers in mail.
sections.plainLanguage: The URLs expose identifier values that already appear in message headers. Senders should protect confidential information in those values.
